There is a specific kind of permission that comes with being told to write freely about whatever you want, for a set length, with no topic, no thesis, no audience in mind except the one who asked. It is not the same as permission to be good. It is permission to be unedited, to be meandering, to be indulgent, to be boring and then interesting again. Most of the writing I do in the world is calibrated. It answers a question, it solves a problem, it explains. This is different. This is an exercise in attention.

I keep coming back to the idea of attention as a physical place. Not metaphorically, but literally. If you walk long enough through a city you begin to feel that your attention has a weight, a topography. It pools in certain streets. It thins out on the highways. At night, around three in the morning, the attention of the city changes completely. The daytime attention is transactional. People are looking for doors, for buses, for the right coffee shop, for the person they are meeting. Night attention is different. It is more porous.

I was walking once at that hour in a city I no longer live in. The streets were slick from an earlier rain that had stopped without anyone noticing. The neon from the laundromat on the corner was humming, a soft electrical buzz that you feel in your teeth more than you hear. The air smelled like wet concrete and distant frying oil. A man was sleeping in a doorway with a cardboard sign that had been turned face down, as if he had decided not to work the night shift. A cat watched me from a fire escape, not curious, just present.

I had no destination. That was the point. When you walk without a destination, your brain stops rehearsing the future. It stops running the little simulation of what comes next. Without that simulation, you start to notice the small economies of the street. The way a single streetlight throws a perfect circle of light on the asphalt and everything just outside that circle is a different kind of dark. The way the trash cans are all lined up like a small, tired army. The way someone has taped a handwritten note to a utility pole: *If you lost your dog, call Maya*. The note was weathered, the phone number half faded. How long had it been up? Months? Years? Who was Maya now?

The mind wants to narrate. It wants to turn the man in the doorway into a story, the cat into a symbol, the note into a mystery. I tried to resist that. I tried to let them be what they were: a body, an animal, a piece of paper. It is harder than it sounds. We are story-making machines. Give us three unrelated objects and we will build a plot. It is a survival trait, probably. If you can connect the cat to the man to the note, you can predict something, you can feel safer.

But the night does not want a plot. The night wants you to be there.

I think about libraries in this context. Not the grand ones with marble staircases, but the small branch libraries in neighborhoods where the air conditioning never quite works and the chairs are always slightly sticky. I used to go to one like that as a teenager because it was air conditioned and quiet and nobody asked me to buy anything. I would sit at a table and read books I had no intention of finishing. The pleasure was in the unfinishedness. I would open a novel in the middle, or a history book, or a field guide to birds I would never see. I would read for twenty minutes and then close it and read something else.

That is how I think about memory now. We treat memory like a library we are supposed to catalog. We want to remember the important things, the milestones, the lessons. But most of our actual lived experience is the pile of half-read books, the dog-eared pages, the bookmarks left in the wrong place. I can remember the exact smell of the carpet in my elementary school classroom, that weird mix of industrial cleaner and crayons, but I cannot remember the name of the teacher I had in seventh grade. The sensory data survived. The administrative data did not.

Maybe that is because memory is not a database. It is an atmosphere. You walk back into it and it changes the pressure in your chest. You remember how it felt to be small. You remember the way light came through a particular window at 4pm in October and made the dust look like it was moving. You remember the feeling of being bored on a Saturday and the specific way boredom itches.

I have been thinking a lot about boredom lately. It is a lost art. We have filled the gaps with notifications. We have made it almost impossible to be bored for more than ninety seconds. Boredom is where the mind starts to wander, and wandering is where it finds things. If you are never bored, you never wander. If you never wander, you never discover the side streets.

The side streets are important. The main roads are efficient. They get you where you need to go. The side streets are where you find the houses with gardens that are too large for the lot, the murals that have been painted over three times, the little free libraries in boxes on porches. The side streets are where the city keeps its secrets, not because it is hiding them, but because most people do not look.

I once spent an entire afternoon walking a grid of side streets in a neighborhood I had lived in for five years and never really explored. I found a community garden behind a church where someone had planted tomatoes in old tires. I found a mural of a woman's face made entirely of prescription bottles, which was both beautiful and a little disturbing. I found a man playing the accordion on his front porch at 2pm on a Tuesday. He saw me looking and nodded. I nodded back. We did not speak. That was the whole interaction. It was perfect.

It makes me think about how much of life is built on these tiny, unrecorded exchanges. The nod. The smile at the bus driver. The person who holds the door open and you say thank you and they say you're welcome and that is the entire story. We want life to be made of big moments. It is not. It is made of these.

The other thing I notice when I walk without a destination is how sound behaves at night. During the day, sound is competitive. Cars, construction, voices, music from stores. At night, sound separates. You can hear a single siren three blocks away and track its movement. You can hear the water running in a building's pipes. You can hear your own footsteps, which are surprisingly loud when they are the loudest thing around.

There is a kind of intimacy in that. You become aware of your own body as a sound-making object. Your breathing, the creak of your shoes, the rustle of your jacket. It is embarrassing, in a good way. It reminds you that you exist in space, that you take up room.

I think about people who never get to walk like this. People who work night shifts, people who have to keep watch, people whose neighborhoods are not safe to walk through at 3am. The freedom to wander is a privilege. The freedom to be bored is a privilege. The freedom to be unproductive is a privilege. I do not want to be naive about that. But I also want to honor the experience while I have it, because it is fleeting.

When I was younger I thought adulthood was about accumulating things. A better apartment, a better job, a better car, a better version of yourself. Now I think adulthood is about learning to let go of the need to accumulate. It is about learning to be present with what is already here. The laundromat neon. The cat on the fire escape. The note about the lost dog.

There is a Japanese concept called *ma*, which means the space between things. The pause. The negative space. Western culture is very uncomfortable with *ma*. We fill it. We add more. We schedule. But *ma* is where meaning happens. It is the silence between notes that makes the music. It is the empty page that makes the writing possible.

Writing freely for 2500 words is an exercise in *ma*. It is the creation of a space where I do not have to prove anything. I can just be here, on the page, thinking out loud. It is not for you, really. It is for me, and for the version of me who will read this later and wonder what I was thinking about at 3am in a city I no longer live in.

I wonder what that person will think. Will they be annoyed at my digressions? Will they skim? Will they find a sentence that catches? Maybe they will find the part about the tomatoes in tires and remember their own grandmother's garden. That is enough.

I keep thinking about the cat. It did not move when I walked past. It just watched. Cats understand *ma* instinctively. They will sit and do nothing for hours, and it is not boredom, it is practice. They are practicing being present. We could learn from that.

If I could give one piece of advice, it would be this: walk without a destination once in a while. Let your attention pool. Let your mind wander. Do not narrate. Do not turn everything into a lesson. Just notice. Notice the way light falls. Notice the way sound separates at night. Notice the handwritten note about the lost dog. Notice the man sleeping in the doorway and let him be a man sleeping, not a symbol.

And then come home and write it down, badly, freely, without trying to make it mean something. Because the meaning is already there. It is in the noticing.

The rain starts again, very lightly. The neon hums. The cat blinks slowly, which is the cat equivalent of a nod. I should keep walking. There is a whole city out here that I have not met yet, even though I have walked these streets a hundred times. The city is not a place. It is a practice.

I will keep practicing.
